quote: In the world of the unenlightened ones, there is authority and un-authority.
content: The essay agrees with Kuhn, Cheney & Weinstock, and says so ahead of time. "When someone has lived their life accustomed to certainty, you can't just say to them, 'Science is probabilistic, just like all other knowledge,'" it warns, and it then spends half its length on the Argument From The Argument From Gray, the multiplist slide itself. It names the error ("the leap from the two-color view to the single-color view, that all grays are the same shade") and prescribes the evaluativist position: "You can have uncertain knowledge of relatively better and relatively worse options, and still choose." That is the stage the developmental literature says few people reach. The essay prescribes that destination and warns against the halfway house, so it is not the cause of the next problem.

quote: They will accept the first half of the statement as a confession of guilt; and dismiss the second half as a flailing attempt to accuse everyone else to avoid judgment.
content: Van der Bles et al. found an asymmetry, and it runs the essay's way. Numeric ranges cost the source almost nothing, while vague verbal acknowledgements of uncertainty reduced trust in both the figure and the source (van der Bles et al. 2020). The essay's closing proposal is based on exactly that difference. Plain "we are not certain," it says, "suggests you know some specific reason for doubt," while quantified doubt does not. The interlocutor's charge is also not expert disagreement. It is "You scientists changed your minds about how gravity works," a charge of revision over time, which the essay answers as a feature. Gustafson & Rice's result, that consensus uncertainty hurts and technical uncertainty mostly does not, is a finer-grained version of the essay's distinction.

quote: If you take one hundred people and ask them each to make a statement of which they are “absolutely certain,” how many of these statements will be correct? Not one hundred.
content: The essay's claim is "Not one hundred." To refute it, a hundred self-chosen certainties would all have to be correct. Fable's own prediction, "near one hundred," concedes the point. The hard-easy effect does not rescue perfect accuracy either. People who pick their own "certain" items reach for widely believed things, and the literature on confidently held misconceptions (the tongue map, the Great Wall seen from orbit, Viking horned helmets) shows those items fail at rates well above zero. Fischhoff, Slovic & Lichtenstein's subjects put odds of a million to one on answers that were wrong several percent of the time (Fischhoff et al. 1977). Ecological sampling reduces that gap without closing it. The essay needs only one error in a hundred, and every version of the experiment supplies it.

quote: If anything, the statements that people are really fanatic about are far less likely to be correct than statements like “the Sun is larger than the Moon” that seem too obvious to get excited about.
content: The argument is in the essay, and it is close to arithmetic. "For every statement you can find of which someone is 'absolutely certain,' you can probably find someone 'absolutely certain' of its opposite." A proposition and its negation cannot both be true, so at most half of a population of fanatically opposed certainties is correct. "The Sun is larger than the Moon" has no opposing fanatics and is right nearly every time it is asserted. "Far less likely" follows from that pairing without a survey. Evolution's defenders do not escape: pooled with the creationists they oppose, fanatical claims about human origins are right about half the time. That pooled figure is what a calibrated reader should expect from heat alone, before looking at the evidence.

quote: it means you think you could make one million equally strong independent statements, one after the other, over the course of a solid year or so, and be wrong, on average, around once
content: Calibration is a Bayesian property, not a frequentist import. Dawid proved that a coherent Bayesian forecaster must expect, by their own lights, to be calibrated: among the occasions on which they assert probability p, the frequency of truth should come out near p (Dawid 1982). The "million statements" gloss spells out that theorem in terms a reader can imagine. It is not a reference-class definition of the credence. It is also no more impossible to run than de Finetti's betting interpretation, which asks for bets nobody places. It is a way to make the number concrete, and the number stays in the mind. The essay's conclusion does not depend on it. It depends on the fact that a human brain has never earned a track record fine enough to justify 1.0.
